mcqs.question: In the CAP theorem, what does "consistency" specifically mean?
options: Every read returns the most recent write, or an error - never stale data
The system never crashes or restarts
All nodes have identical hardware specifications
The system responds within a fixed time limit
mcqs.explanation: CAP's consistency means reads always reflect the latest acknowledged write (or fail rather than return something stale). It has nothing to do with hardware uniformity, uptime, or response-time guarantees - those are separate concerns.

mcqs.question: During a network partition between nodes A and B, why can't node B simply return the correct latest value written to node A?
options: Node B has no way to learn A's latest value while the network connecting them is cut - it's not an engineering gap, it's what a partition means
Node B is intentionally programmed to always be slightly out of date
Only node A is allowed to serve read requests in any distributed system
Node B would need to restart before it could receive updates
mcqs.explanation: During a genuine partition, no message can cross the cut - so B literally cannot know what A did, regardless of how well-engineered the system is. This isn't about intentional staleness, read-routing rules, or restarts; it's the definition of network partition.

mcqs.question: What is wrong with the common phrasing "CAP means pick any 2 of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance"?
options: It's completely correct and is the best way to describe CAP
CAP theorem doesn't apply to any real production database
Partition tolerance isn't an optional design choice for a real distributed system - the actual forced choice is between C and A, and only during an actual partition
The theorem actually has four properties, not three
mcqs.explanation: Real networks fail, so partition tolerance isn't something you can opt out of if you're actually distributed - a 'CA' system just means a single node. The genuine, narrower choice CAP forces is C vs A, and specifically while a partition is happening. CAP has exactly three named properties and does apply broadly to distributed systems.

mcqs.question: Two systems are both classified as AP under CAP. Why might they still behave very differently day-to-day, according to PACELC?
options: AP systems are always identical in every other respect
Even with the same partition-time choice, they can differ in the normal (non-partitioned) case by trading latency against consistency differently
PACELC only applies to CP systems, not AP ones
The difference would only show up in how they handle disk failures
mcqs.explanation: CAP's A/C choice only describes partition-time behavior. PACELC adds the 'Else' case: absent a partition, a system still chooses between lower latency (acknowledging fast, replicating async) and stronger consistency (waiting for confirmation). Two AP systems can land differently there. PACELC applies to any system, not just CP ones, and this isn't specifically about disk failures.

mcqs.question: DynamoDB defaults to eventually consistent reads but offers a per-query ConsistentRead option for a strongly consistent read. What does this reveal about labeling a database simply "AP" or "CP"?
options: The label is meaningless and should never be used
The C-vs-A trade-off can be a per-operation choice within the same system, not a single fixed property of the whole database
DynamoDB is actually CP, and the AP label is simply incorrect
This option only exists for writes, never for reads
mcqs.explanation: A single system can expose different consistency trade-offs per call — DynamoDB's default is AP-flavored but a specific query can opt into a CP-flavored strongly consistent read. The label isn't meaningless (it describes the default), DynamoDB isn't simply mislabeled as AP, and the example given is specifically about consistent reads, not writes.
